e.t: Abioud, also rendered Aviuth, is a personal name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name when it appears in a sentence. The name occurs 13 times across 13 verses in the LXX corpus, from Exodus through 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific family or historical role cannot be stated here, but its ordinary lexical function is to name a person.

This noun refers to garrulity—excessive, empty, or idle talk. It describes speech marked more by needless words than by useful substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, so it represents a recurring biblical concern about talk that lacks purpose or value. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains speech that is frivolous, wordy, or unhelpful.

Azarion is a personal name, referring to a specific individual rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Kings 2:46. The name itself identifies the person, but the available lexical information does not provide an additional meaning or description of him. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

This noun means “thistle,” referring to a prickly plant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 14:9. Its basic meaning identifies a plant rather than an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain any figurative or contextual force it may have there; the word itself carries the ordinary sense of a thistle.

This adjective describes something that is not shared with another person or group. It can identify something kept apart from participation, fellowship, or common use, though the precise application depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, at Wisdom 14:21. Its basic meaning remains focused on separation from what others share, rather than describing the reason for that separation or the feelings connected with it.

This adjective means “speaking a foreign language.” It describes someone who speaks in a language different from the one normally understood by the listener. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 3:6, so its basic sense is clear even though this word has a very limited occurrence record. Its focus is language difference: the speaker is foreign-language-speaking in relation to those hearing or being addressed.

This word is a proper name, appearing as “Ambakoum” or “Amvakum.” It functions as a personal name rather than a description, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs nine times, with occurrences connected to Habakkuk and Bel and the Dragon. The name appears in Habakkuk 1:1 and 3:1 and also in several places in Bel and the Dragon. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse.

Ammioud is a personal name, also rendered “Ammiuth.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:4. The available lexical sense is limited to the name itself, so its precise identity and role must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone. This is a Greek LXX name and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament word or as a common vocabulary term.

This adjective means “immense,” describing something extraordinarily great in size, extent, or scale. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), at 3 Maccabees 1:28. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense is clear: it points to something vast or beyond ordinary measure.

Anōch, also rendered Anokh, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its significance is its role as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament, and the available lexical information does not provide an additional meaning or interpretation for the name itself. This LXX word occurs once, in Joshua 15:43. Understanding what the named reference represents requires the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This verb means “wean”: to bring a nursing child to the point of no longer depending on breast milk. It describes a practical change in a child’s nourishment and care, and its use in the Greek Old Testament is limited to eight occurrences. The word can therefore refer to the completion of nursing, whether spoken of directly in family life or used in a comparison. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adverb means “thoughtlessly”: it describes an action done without careful thought or consideration. It tells the reader how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense is acting carelessly instead of with deliberate attention.

Arna is a proper name appearing in the Greek Septuagint. It functions as a personal name rather than as a general description, action, or quality. The name occurs seven times in the Septuagint’s Old Testament corpus, across seven verses. Because the available wording identifies only the name itself and does not provide verse text or further definition, its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This word means “male,” identifying a person or animal as male. It can function either as a noun for a male or as an adjective describing something male. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 53 times, including descriptions of human beings, animals, and sacrificial animals. Its central sense remains consistent across these uses: the male sex, distinguished from the female. The word appears from Genesis through later biblical writings, showing ordinary descriptive use rather than a specialized meaning.

Asyberi, also rendered Asiviri, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named individual or designation in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not establish more about the person or group named. This LXX form occurs once, in Numbers 26:42. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This adjective means “dishonored”: regarded as lacking honor, respect, or good standing. It describes a person or thing treated as disgraceful, insignificant, or unworthy of esteem. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word is used for conditions of social shame or rejection rather than honor and recognition. It occurs 11 times in this LXX corpus, across books including Job, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage says about the person or thing being described.

This adverb means “on the spot,” referring to a place where something happens or to action taken immediately at that location. It points to what occurs right there, rather than elsewhere or at a later time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears five times, including once in Joshua and four times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a sentence depends on whether it describes a location, an immediate response, or an event occurring directly at that place.

Achimōth is a proper name, rendered as “Achimōth” or “Akhimoth.” It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 6:10. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise genealogical role cannot be stated here, but its lexical function is clear: it is a personal name.

This word means “2; beth.” It functions as an unchanging numerical designation, identifying the second position or item, while also naming beth. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:9. Because the available meaning is brief and the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that heading or passage must be understood from its surrounding context. Its basic sense remains a marker for the second entry, associated with beth.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Banaibakat” or “Vanevakat.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:45. Because proper names normally identify people or places rather than translate into an ordinary descriptive meaning, its significance depends on the surrounding passage and the entity it names. The available lexical information preserves the name in these two forms.

“Basi” is a proper name, also identified as “Vasi.” It refers to a person named in the Greek Old Testament text, rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Ezra 2:49. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the name’s specific role in that listing should be understood from Ezra 2:49 itself.

This word is a proper name rendered “Boubastos” or “Vuvastos.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 30:17. The available information gives the name and its spelling variants, but not enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the entity’s role in that passage. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding context of Ezekiel 30.

Gamzō, also rendered Gamzo, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 28:18. The available wording preserves the name itself but does not establish from the name alone whether it identifies a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding passage.

Geth, also written Yeth, is a proper name. It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 35 times across 31 verses, including passages in Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles. The English rendering “Geth” preserves the name rather than translating it as a descriptive word. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Daman, also rendered Thaman, is a proper name. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Jeremiah 47:1. The available lexical meaning identifies it as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the exact person, place, or reference intended at that point cannot be clarified from the word alone. Its significance in Jeremiah 47:1 must therefore be understood from that passage’s context.

e.h: A Word for Speak A Second Time
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “speak a second time”. It describes repeating an act of speaking rather than introducing a different kind of speech. In the Greek Old Testament translation tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:22. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be described further; its lexical meaning remains clear.

This verb means “run across,” describing movement quickly from one side or place to another. It is an action word, so it portrays someone or something traveling across a space rather than merely remaining in motionless presence. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs four times, in three Old Testament passages and once in Wisdom. The surrounding verse determines what is being crossed and why, but the central idea remains movement across a space.

Glory refers to honor, splendor, or exalted greatness that rightly belongs to someone or something. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun is used broadly for the recognized majesty and dignity associated with God, people, or things of great worth. Its central idea is visible or acknowledged excellence that calls for honor. This word occurs 405 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing that glory is a recurring biblical theme rather than a rare expression.

This verb means to have cravings—to experience a strong desire for something. It describes an inward appetite or longing rather than a simple action of taking or receiving. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in three verses in Genesis. Its occurrences belong to the language of desire connected with animals and their breeding, but the word itself chiefly expresses the experience of craving. The surrounding verse determines precisely what is desired and how that desire functions in the sentence.

This Greek verb means “be.” It expresses the state, condition, or existence of a person, thing, or situation. In a sentence, it can connect someone or something with a description or identify what someone or something is. It is a common verb in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 551 times, so its precise force is determined by the surrounding words and sentence. The word appears throughout the Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, serving as a basic way to express being.

This verb means “leave off” or “cease”: it describes something stopping, ending, or no longer continuing. It can refer to an action coming to an end or to something failing to remain. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 159 times, showing that it is used broadly for cessation rather than for one narrow situation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is said to be stopping or coming to an end.

This adjective describes someone or something as “in madness” or “frantic.” It points to an intense, disturbed state rather than ordinary thought or behavior. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in Wisdom 14:23. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise force in that sentence must be determined from the passage itself, while its basic meaning remains a description of madness or frantic conduct.

This Greek LXX noun refers to what is in the fore or positioned in front. It describes a location or forward part rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Samuel 5:4, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its basic sense remains a positional one: the front area or something situated before another thing. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely what it identifies there.

Ennom is a proper name used to identify a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader definition; its meaning is the name itself, “Ennom.” The name occurs five times, appearing once in 2 Kings and four times in Jeremiah. Its precise referent and significance in each passage depend on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This verb means to make oneself equal—to present oneself as equal to another or to something else. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 32:9. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the act of making oneself equal. This word belongs to the Greek LXX corpus and should not be confused with a Greek New Testament word merely because the languages are related.

This verb means “drive,” describing the act of forcing or moving someone or something away. It presents action rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 27 times, so its basic sense appears across a range of passages involving removal or movement. The surrounding words determine whether the driving is forceful, protective, or directed toward another destination; the core idea remains causing someone or something to go away.

This Greek LXX verb means “ashamed”: it describes experiencing or expressing shame. As a verb, it presents shame as something a person feels or acknowledges rather than as a fixed description of a person. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains the experience of being ashamed.

This Greek LXX verb means “fix on; hold on.” It describes directing attention toward something or maintaining a firm hold, depending on how it functions in its sentence. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense appears across more than one kind of passage. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on focusing attention or holding firmly.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn around; return.” It describes moving back, turning toward something again, or going back to a previous place or direction. The word occurs 491 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so its basic sense is broad and regularly used for physical movement. Depending on the sentence, it may describe a person returning, turning back, or changing direction. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Esabana, also rendered Esavana, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nehemiah 10:26. Since this name is preserved as a personal designation and no broader definition is supplied, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it names an individual in the biblical record. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb refers to a comrade or to comrade-like association. It describes the idea of relating to someone as a companion or associate, rather than naming an object or place. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 9:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning is the presence or role of a comrade.

This noun means “prosperity”—a condition of flourishing, abundance, or material well-being. It describes favorable plenty rather than a person, action, or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times across ten verses, including several passages in Genesis 41 and others in Psalms and Ezekiel. Its precise shade depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains prosperity or flourishing.

This adjective describes someone or something as “sweetly-speaking”—using speech that is pleasant, gentle, or appealing to hear. It points to the character of a person’s words rather than naming an action or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Job and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the word highlights a speaker, the quality of speech, or its pleasing effect.

Echran is a proper name, rendered “Echran” and also given as “Ekhran.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs five times in the LXX, all in Numbers, including references in Numbers 1, 2, 7, and 10. Its precise personal identity and role require the surrounding verse and passage.

Zoath is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea, so its meaning is primarily its identity as a name. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX text, both within 1 Chronicles 4:20. The surrounding verse text would be needed to identify exactly whom or what Zoath names there.

Thedmor, also rendered Thethmor, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Chronicles 8:4. The reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what the name refers to in that passage.

This Greek noun means “tempest,” referring to a powerful storm or turbulent wind. It names a weather disturbance rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus and Deuteronomy. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a tempest: a storm marked by intense, unsettled movement.

This Greek LXX noun means “breastplate,” a piece of armor worn over the chest for protection. It refers to defensive body armor rather than to a person or an abstract quality. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, appearing in descriptions of military equipment and armor. Its basic sense remains the same wherever it occurs: a protective covering for the chest. The surrounding verse determines the particular scene, but the word itself identifies the armor being worn or used.

Iambri is a proper name, also rendered Iamvri. It identifies a particular person or named figure in the Greek text of 1 Maccabees. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 9:36 and 9:37. Since the available wording does not include the surrounding verses, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s role, character, or actions. Its meaning is therefore best expressed as the personal name Iambri, or Iamvri.

This word means “ibis,” an Egyptian bird. It is a noun used for the bird itself, not for an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy, in passages that identify birds by name. The word therefore gives a specific name for a recognizable bird rather than a broad term for birds generally. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and the larger list in which it appears.

This noun means “sacrilegious plunder”: the taking or spoiling of something sacred in a way that dishonors its holy character. It names a profane seizure rather than ordinary theft, focusing on the violation of what belongs to the sacred sphere. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:39. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “lace,” referring to a narrow fastening or tie. It appears five times across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, including Job, Isaiah, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains consistent as the name of a lace or fastening used in ordinary descriptions. The exact force of the word in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself carries this simple, concrete meaning.

This adjective describes something as forceful or severe. It can express strength, intensity, or a demanding quality, depending on the noun or situation it describes. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 136 times, so it is used across a broad range of passages rather than for one narrow subject. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding words and context.

This conjunction means “also I” or “and that,” linking its words to what has already been said. It can add the speaker or another point, or connect a further statement introduced by “that.” Its role is connective rather than descriptive: it joins parts of a sentence and helps carry the thought forward. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:10. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which connective sense is active there.

This Greek LXX verb means “burn up”: to consume something with fire until it is burned. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its ordinary sense remains direct and physical. The word occurs 96 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing repeated use for things being consumed or destroyed by burning. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “cleave asunder” or “split up,” describing the act of separating something into distinct parts. It presents division as an action rather than merely a condition of being divided. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 1:56. The precise force of the action in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself centers on forceful separation or cutting apart.

Ostentation is a noun describing a showy display intended to attract attention or admiration. It points to outward impressiveness rather than quiet simplicity, especially when someone makes a display of possessions, status, or achievement. This Greek LXX word occurs three times in the deuterocanonical writings represented here, appearing in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kiras is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:47, and is rendered “Kiras.” Because it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes one individual within the passage. The word does not provide a broader common meaning such as a virtue, event, or spiritual quality.

This noun means a “paneled ceiling”—a ceiling finished with fitted or decorative panels. It refers to an architectural feature rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Haggai 1:4. The word’s precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is a ceiling constructed or covered with panels.

The word refers to a “folded garment”—a piece of clothing arranged by folding. It is a noun that names an object rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 43:13. Its particular significance in that passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains a garment identified by its folded arrangement.

This Greek LXX noun means “decision” or “judgment”: a determination made about a matter, including the judgment reached in a legal or moral case. It can refer to the act or result of deciding rightly between matters. The word appears 252 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it has broad use rather than describing only one kind of ruling. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “lantern,” referring to a portable light used to illuminate darkness. It is a noun, naming an object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 15 times, with uses spread across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 15:17, and it also appears in Exodus, Judges, Daniel, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees. The precise significance of a lantern in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

This adverb means “like a lion,” describing something done or appearing in a lion-like manner. It expresses resemblance to a lion rather than naming a lion itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is a comparison: something is characterized by the manner, appearance, or quality associated with a lion.

Magdōlos is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general quality or action. It is also represented as “Magtholos.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, both times in Jeremiah: once at Jeremiah 26:14 and once at Jeremiah 51:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the name’s particular reference cannot be identified more precisely here, but its basic function is that of a named entity.

Makelloth is a proper name, rendered “Makellōth” or “Makelloth.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available wording does not establish which kind of name it is. This name occurs twice in the Greek text of 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 9:37 and 9:38. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes Makelloth from other people, places, or families named in the surrounding genealogical record.

Maon is a proper name, rendered as “Maon.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used to identify a particular person, place, or other named entity in the Old Testament Greek text. It occurs three times in two verses, appearing twice in 1 Chronicles 2:45 and once in Jeremiah 31:23. The supplied lexical information identifies the name but does not specify its referent in each passage.

“Mēdias; Mithias” is a proper name, identifying a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees: 1 Maccabees 6:56 and 14:2. The lexical information establishes the name itself, while its particular role or significance must be determined from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

Molchol is a proper name, also rendered “Molkhol.” The available lexical information identifies it as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 2 Kings 23:13 and once in 1 Chronicles 20:2. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity or role cannot be stated more precisely, but its basic function is to designate a particular named entity.

Nabōk, also rendered Navok, is a proper name preserved as a personal or place name rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:33. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its precise referent must be determined from that passage. The name itself carries no additional lexical meaning in the available record.

This Greek LXX verb means “diseased,” describing a person or condition affected by illness. It functions as an action or state word: someone or something is unwell rather than healthy. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both within one verse in Wisdom 17:8. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise force in that passage depends on its context.

This word means “cup-bearer,” a person whose role involved serving or presenting a ruler’s drink. It functions as a noun describing an attendant or court servant, though it can also modify a person associated with that duty. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, including passages in Genesis, Kings, Chronicles, Nehemiah, and Ecclesiastes. The word’s basic meaning remains focused on the office or service of a cup-bearer rather than on the drink itself.

This word means “whensoever”. It is a conjunction that points to a time or circumstance, introducing something that may happen whenever a stated condition or occasion occurs. In ordinary English, it connects an event with the time related to it, rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it appears once, in Job 29:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic function remains a time-related connector meaning “whensoever”.

Ochozian, also rendered Okhozian, is a proper name for a person in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint). It does not describe a quality, action, or general idea; it identifies someone by name. The name occurs four times in the LXX, in 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles, including 2 Kings 9:23 and three passages in 2 Chronicles. The person's specific role cannot be stated reliably without the surrounding verse text.

This noun means “celebration of a feast,” referring to a joyful observance or gathering centered on a feast. It names the celebration itself rather than a person, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:12, so its meaning is presented through this focused lexical sense rather than a broad range of repeated uses. The word describes festive observance in general, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular force there.

This Greek LXX verb means “paralyze”: to disable or deprive someone of the strength to move or act. It describes an action that leaves a person or force unable to function normally. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is established across multiple passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on what or whom the action affects.

This Greek LXX noun means “comfort,” referring to support or consolation that brings relief and encouragement. It names comfort as something given or received, rather than describing an action by itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning remains the strengthening or consolation offered to someone in distress or difficulty.

This LXX Greek verb means “persuade”: to move someone toward agreement, acceptance, or confidence. It describes the act of influencing another person through speech or appeal rather than simply stating information. The word appears 170 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a well-attested verb in this corpus. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on who is persuading, whom they address, and the surrounding words.

This noun means “preservation”: the act or result of being kept safe, guarded, or maintained. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, each in a different verse, so its basic sense is clear even though its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. The word points to something being preserved from loss, ruin, or harm rather than simply created or acquired. It can therefore describe the keeping of people, blessings, or an intended condition according to the context.

This adjective means “most,” describing the greatest number or highest degree among people or things. It is a comparison word: it identifies what exceeds the others in amount or extent. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses across 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what group or quality it compares, but its central sense remains the highest or greatest portion.

This noun means “spirit” or “wind,” referring either to an unseen spiritual reality or to moving air, as the surrounding passage determines. It is a broad word used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related books, appearing 329 times in this LXX corpus. Its uses include references to God’s Spirit, a person’s inner spirit, spiritual beings, and the wind, but the exact sense must be determined from each verse’s context.

This word means “leek,” the name of a vegetable. It is a noun used to identify that food, not an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Numbers 11:5. Its meaning is straightforward and concrete: it refers to the leek plant or the food made from it. The surrounding verse would determine how the word functions in that particular sentence, but the word itself carries this simple everyday meaning.

This verb means “appear besides”: it describes someone or something coming into view alongside another person or thing. It is an action word, so it focuses on the act of appearing rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:26. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.
